messages.subject: Evaluate condition of 'if' statement
parts:
Hi everyone,

I’m new to Nimble and have some prior experience programming in Stan. While Stan has been great, I’ve encountered some modeling scenarios that it couldn’t handle but Nimble seems capable of addressing.

Recently, I translated a model I previously wrote in Stan into Nimble, but I ran into the following error:

Defining model
Error in eval(code[[2]], constantsEnv) : object 'inf_time' not found
Error in codeProcessIfThenElse(code[[i]], constants, envir) :
  Cannot evaluate condition of 'if' statement: inf_time[i] >= t || inf_time[i] == -1.
Condition must be able to be evaluated based on values in 'constants'.

Below is the full code I’m working with. The model iterates over days and the population to calculate the probability of infection. The infection variable is a matrix that records whether each individual is infected on each day (0 for not infected, 1 for infected).

Code <- nimbleCode({
    alpha ~ dgamma(1.5, 1)          
    beta ~ dgamma(2, 3)    
    delta1 ~ dgamma(1, 1)        
    delta2 ~ dgamma(1, 1)      
    num_inf<-1
    for (t in t_start:t_end) {
      at_1 <- 1 - exp(-delta1 * num_inf)
      at_2 <- 1 - exp(-delta2 * num_inf)  
      beta_adj <- beta * pow((1 - at_2), -1)
      for (i in 1:N) {
        if(inf_time[i]>=t || inf_time[i]==-1){
          kernel[i, t] <- 0
          for (j in 1:N) {
            if (i != j && inf_time[j]!=-1 && inf_time[j]<t && inf_time[j]+t_rem>=t) {
              d <- sqrt(pow((x[i] - x[j]), 2) + pow((y[i] - y[j]), 2))
              kernel[i, t] <- kernel[i, t] + pow((d + 1), -beta_adj)
            }
          }
          prob[i, t] <- 1 - exp(-(alpha * (1 - at_1)) * kernel[i, t])
          infection[i, t] ~ dbern(prob[i, t])
          if(inf_time[i]==t){
            num_inf <- num_inf + 1
          }
        }
        else if (inf_time[i]+t_rem==t) {
          num_inf <- num_inf - 1
        }
      }
    }
  })
##Nimble model
Model <- nimbleModel(Code,
                     data = list(y = data$position_y,
                                 x = data$position_x,
                                 infection = infection_matrix(data$time_of_infected, 30),
                                 inf_time = data$time_of_infected),
                     constants = list(N = 100, t_start = 1, t_end = 30, t_rem = 3),
                     inits = list(alpha = 1, beta = 1, delta1 = 0, delta2 = 0.001))

I also tried pre-calculating the kernels (used in the infection probability calculation) to optimize the model. However, I realized that the calculation depends on parameter \beta, as it is used in the power of the distance. 

Thanks in advance for any comments and thoughts! Apologies if this question is too basic—I’m still learning! 😊

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Evaluate condition of 'if' statement
parts:
Dear Miki,

Thanks for posting the question and welcome to nimble.

I think there might be some basics for you to get up to speed on about nimble models. The model code declares relationships among nodes in a directed acyclic graph. For you coming from Stan, this is quite different. Stan and most programming involves step-by-step instructions, re-using variables and so on (imperative programming). nimble's model language is declarative. That means the code is processed to determine the known set of relationships among nodes, and the order of declarations does not matter. For this reason, if-then-else is not supported (well it is supported but in a different way, to include or exclude blocks of code for the entire model, not differently for iterations in a for loop). And a node can't be declared twice, such as "num_inf <- 1" and later "num_inf <- num_inf + 1". That would mean the same node appears in the model graph twice, which can't happen. num_inf (or any other node) can only have one declared relationship. nimble's algorithms can then use the DAG relationships in setting up calculations.

Sometimes, what people want to do with if-then-else can instead be achieved by nested indexing. e.g.
for(i in 1:n) {
  x[k[i]] <- {some equation}
}
where k[i] is provided in the constants list and determines in advance which of the x[i] should have this declaration.

In your case, while I am not trying to follow your code in full detail, it appears that the for loop iterations are more involved. In that case, you can put them in a nimbleFunction and use that in the model. For example, you could replace the entire nested for loops with

infection[1:N, t_start:t_end] ~ d_my_model_log_probs(delta1, delta2, alpha, beta )

Then in the nimbleFunction d_my_model_log_probs you would calculate the sum of log probabilities of all the infection[,] data using your for loops. We call this a user-defined distribution.

At this point I'll encourage you to look up user-defined distributions in our user manual at r-nimble.org. After you've explored more, feel free to ask more.

Perry
